summary: Revises RFC 2086, which lets IMAP mailbox access control lists be read and changed over the protocol. It defines several new access control rights and clarifies which rights are needed for different IMAP commands. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4314 defines how an IMAP server lets users inspect and change mailbox permissions. It clarifies which permission each command needs and preserves compatibility with clients that use the earlier rules.

subtitle: A revised IMAP extension for listing and changing mailbox permissions.

tldr.problem: The earlier IMAP ACL extension left unclear which permissions commands need and how identifiers and older rights should work.
tldr.mechanism: Servers advertise ACL support and manage identifier-right pairs with SETACL, DELETEACL, GETACL, LISTRIGHTS, and MYRIGHTS. Each standard right controls specified mailbox or message actions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4314 replaces RFC 2086, defines finer rights, and keeps virtual c and d rights for compatibility with older clients.

today: RFC 4314 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005 and obsoletes RFC 2086. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The ACL Extension
sections.content:
The Access Control List (ACL) extension lets an IMAP client retrieve and change permissions on mailboxes. A server advertises support by including ACL in its CAPABILITY response.

RFC 4314 revises RFC 2086. It clarifies UTF-8 access identifiers, command permissions, and how ACL rights relate to IMAP's READ-WRITE and READ-ONLY response codes.
sections.plainLanguage: The ACL extension lets an IMAP client ask who may use a mailbox and change those permissions. This revision clarifies rules that were ambiguous in the earlier specification.

sections.title: Identifiers and Standard Rights
sections.content:
An ACL is a set of identifier-and-rights pairs attached to a mailbox. Identifiers are UTF-8 strings; anyone means every identity, including anonymous users. A right is a lowercase letter representing permitted operations, while digits are reserved for site-defined rights.

Standard rights include l for listing a mailbox, r for reading it, i for adding messages, and a for ACL administration. The server determines how rights from multiple matching identifiers combine; MYRIGHTS reports the current user's rights.

An identifier beginning with a dash can specify negative rights, which remove a right granted by another matching entry. Servers are not required to support negative rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mailbox permission links an identifier to a set of rights. The letters stand for actions, and the server reports which rights apply to the current user.

sections.title: Virtual Rights for Older Clients
sections.content:
The old extension used c and d ambiguously for mailbox creation and deletion. RFC 4314 separates these actions: k controls creating mailboxes, x controls deleting them, e controls expunging, and t controls the Deleted flag.

The server continues to accept virtual c and d rights as combinations of the newer rights. When returning ACL or MYRIGHTS data, it includes the corresponding virtual right when one of its component rights is granted. New clients ignore these virtual rights in responses.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rights separate actions that older clients treated as one permission. Servers keep accepting the old c and d rights so those clients can continue to work.

sections.title: Commands for Managing Permissions
sections.content:
SETACL adds, removes, or replaces rights for an identifier. DELETEACL removes that identifier's entry, and GETACL returns the whole list. An unrecognized right in SETACL MUST cause a BAD response rather than being silently ignored.

LISTRIGHTS reports rights that can be granted to an identifier, including rights the server always grants and groups of rights that must be granted together. MYRIGHTS reports the current user's rights on a mailbox.

For commands that accept an identifier, servers SHOULD prepare it using SASLprep. They MUST reject it with BAD if preparation fails or produces an empty string.
sections.plainLanguage: Five commands let a client change an ACL, remove an entry, read the list, inspect possible rights, or check its own rights. The server must reject permission letters it does not recognize.

sections.title: Rights Required by IMAP Commands
sections.content:
An ACL server MUST check the required rights before executing a command. LIST needs l; SELECT, EXAMINE, and STATUS need r; and EXPUNGE needs e. ACL management commands need a.

CREATE needs k on the nearest existing parent mailbox. DELETE needs x; RENAME needs x on the mailbox and k on its new parent. APPEND and COPY need i on the target mailbox.

When copying or appending, the server stores each message flag only if the user has its matching right: t for Deleted, s for Seen, and w for other flags. It MUST NOT fail the whole operation just because a flag cannot be stored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IMAP action has a required permission, such as read, insert, or administer. When a copied message has a flag the user cannot set, the server can omit that flag without failing the copy.

sections.title: Server and Client Behavior
sections.content:
Servers MUST advertise extra rights in the RIGHTS= capability, including t, e, x, and k. They MUST report the current user's rights accurately in FLAGS and PERMANENTFLAGS responses.

A server may cache rights while a mailbox is selected, so a permission change may take effect only after reselection. If an ACL change also changes other entries, the server MUST send ACL responses describing those changes.

A client that edits ACLs but cannot edit unfamiliar rights MUST preserve those rights when saving changes. Otherwise it could remove permissions the user did not see.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers must advertise extra rights and report the user's current permissions accurately. Clients must preserve unfamiliar rights when they save an ACL.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ACL commands MUST NOT reveal that a restricted mailbox exists. For example, GETACL on a mailbox the user cannot list should return the same error as a request for a nonexistent mailbox.

Clients SHOULD warn before granting full access or the a right to anyone. ACL information is sent without confidentiality unless STARTTLS, negotiated privacy in AUTHENTICATE, or another protection mechanism is used.
sections.plainLanguage: A server must not reveal a hidden mailbox through ACL commands. Clients should warn before granting administrative access to everyone, and the connection needs protection to keep ACL data confidential.
